lead: Some plastics carry current. A conducting polymer has a backbone of alternating single and double bonds, so its π electrons are delocalised along the chain. Chemical doping — oxidation or reduction — creates charged defects called polarons and bipolarons. These charges move along the chain and hop between chains, turning an insulator into a conductor. Conductivities reach 10<sup>3</sup> S/cm, far below copper but enough for antistatic coatings, sensors, OLEDs, electromagnetic interference shielding and supercapacitor electrodes.
prereq: You need 5.1 for the polymer chain, and Unit 6 for the band picture of solids.

blocks.text: A polymer chain is conjugated when its carbon atoms alternate single and double bonds: –CH=CH–CH=CH–. Each double bond contributes a π bond. The p orbitals on neighbouring carbons overlap sideways, so the π electrons are not fixed to one pair of atoms; they spread over the whole conjugated segment. This delocalisation gives the chain a gap of a few electronvolts, so long conjugated segments absorb visible light and the polymer looks coloured; short segments absorb in the ultraviolet. The same delocalisation lets the chain carry charge.

In trans-polyacetylene, the simplest conjugated polymer, the single and double bonds alternate in a regular pattern. This bond alternation opens an energy gap between the filled π band and the empty π* band. The gap is about 1.5 eV. At room temperature only a tiny fraction of electrons can cross a 1.5 eV gap, so undoped trans-polyacetylene is an insulator. The gap is the polymer version of the band gap in a semiconductor; see Unit 6.

The gap is small enough to modify by chemistry. Adding or removing a few electrons per chain creates new electronic levels inside the gap. Those levels are the resting places for the charges that carry current after doping.

Doping here means chemical oxidation or reduction of the conjugated chain, not adding impurity atoms to a semiconductor lattice. In p-type doping the chain is oxidised: electrons are removed. Iodine vapour is the classic oxidant for polyacetylene. In n-type doping the chain is reduced: electrons are added, for example by sodium. The counter-ion sits nearby to keep the film neutral overall.

Removing one electron creates a radical cation on the chain: one positive charge and one unpaired electron. This defect is a polaron. Removing a second electron near the same place gives a bipolaron: two positive charges with no unpaired electron. Both distort the chain locally and produce levels inside the gap. A polaron or bipolaron can move along the chain by shifting the bond pattern, and it can hop from one chain to the next.

Conductivity σ is quoted in siemens per centimetre (S/cm); 1 S/cm = 100 S/m. Undoped conjugated polymers are near 10<sup>−10</sup> S/cm. Doped films reach 10<sup>−3</sup> to 10<sup>3</sup> S/cm, and the best samples approach 10<sup>5</sup> S/cm. Between chains, hopping is the weak step, so order and morphology matter.

Thin films are measured by the four-probe method. Four contacts sit in a line; the outer two pass a current I, and the inner two measure the voltage V. This avoids errors from contact resistance. Most conducting polymers are intractable — they do not melt or dissolve easily — so they are processed as dispersions, such as PEDOT:PSS in water.

items: Polyaniline: made from aniline, cheap and stable. Acid doping gives a green conducting salt. Uses: antistatic coatings on packaging and electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding, where a conductive layer blocks stray radio signals.
Polypyrrole: formed by electropolymerisation as a tough film. Uses: gas and glucose sensors, and supercapacitor electrodes that store charge at the polymer surface.

PEDOT:PSS: the conducting polymer PEDOT (poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)) charge-balanced by the polyanion PSS (polystyrene sulfonate), supplied as a water dispersion. Uses: transparent hole-injecting layer in organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), and antistatic coatings.

blocks.text: The common thread is a conjugated backbone plus a dopant. Dopant level, chain order and processing decide the final conductivity. A film for an antistatic bag needs only slight conduction; a supercapacitor electrode needs high surface area and fast ion access; an OLED layer needs transparency and the right work function.

examples.question: A doped polyaniline film is 2.0 cm long, 1.0 cm wide and 0.10 cm thick. Its resistance along the length is 40 Ω. Find the conductivity in S/cm and in S/m. Compare with copper, about 10<sup>5</sup> S/cm.
steps: The cross-section area is A = width × thickness = 1.0 cm × 0.10 cm = 0.10 cm².
Resistance is R = ρ l / A, so resistivity ρ = R A / l. Conductivity σ = 1/ρ = l / (R A).
Convert: 1 S/cm = 100 S/m, so σ = 0.50 × 100 = 50 S/m.
Copper is about 10<sup>5</sup> S/cm, which is 2 × 10<sup>5</sup> times larger than 0.50 S/cm. The film conducts, but it is far below a metal.
examples.answer: The film conductivity is 0.50 S/cm (50 S/m); copper is about 2 × 10<sup>5</sup> times more conductive.
examples.check:
l = 2.0
w = 1.0
t = 0.10
R = 40.0
A = w * t
sigma = l / (R * A)
print(f'{A:.2f}')
print(f'{sigma:.2f}')
print(f'{sigma*100:.1f}')

traps: Doping is chemical oxidation or reduction of the chain. It is not the addition of impurity atoms to a semiconductor lattice; that is semiconductor doping in Unit 6.
p-type means the polymer chain loses electrons and becomes positively charged. Do not read p as positive holes added from outside; the oxidant removes electrons.
S/cm and S/m differ by a factor of 100: 1 S/cm = 100 S/m. Convert before comparing with copper.
A polaron is a radical cation (or radical anion), not just a bare charge. A bipolaron has two charges and no unpaired electron.
High doping does not always mean high conductivity. Too much dopant can distort chains, reduce order, and lower mobility.

quiz.q: What structural feature must a polymer backbone have to be conjugated?
quiz.a: It must have alternating single and double bonds, so the p orbitals overlap and the π electrons are delocalised along the chain.

quiz.q: Define p-type and n-type doping of a conducting polymer.
quiz.a: p-type doping is oxidation: electrons are removed from the chain. n-type doping is reduction: electrons are added to the chain.

quiz.q: Why is undoped trans-polyacetylene an insulator even though its π electrons are delocalised?
quiz.a: Bond alternation opens a gap of about 1.5 eV between the filled π band and the empty π* band. At room temperature few electrons can cross this gap, so there are few charge carriers.

quiz.q: What is a bipolaron and how does it differ from a polaron?
quiz.a: A bipolaron is two charges paired on the chain with no unpaired electron. A polaron is one charge plus one unpaired electron, so it is a radical ion.

quiz.q: A doped polypyrrole film is 5.0 cm long, 2.0 cm wide and 0.050 cm thick. Its resistance along the length is 100 Ω. Find σ in S/cm.
Why does interchain hopping limit conductivity in a conducting polymer film?
quiz.a: Charges move quickly along a conjugated chain but must jump between chains. Disorder, poor chain contacts and insulating side groups raise the barrier to hopping, so the film conductivity is lower than along a single chain.

quiz.q: A student measures a film with two probes and gets a lower conductivity than with four probes. Explain.
quiz.a: Two-probe resistance includes contact resistance and wire resistance in series with the film. Four-probe measurement passes current through the outer contacts and measures voltage across the inner contacts, so contact resistance is not included.

beyond: Not for the exam. Conducting polymer research now includes stretchable bioelectrodes, organic electrochemical transistors, and printed electronics. PEDOT:PSS dispersions are used in roll-to-roll coating for flexible devices. Search for organic electrochemical transistor, conducting polymer dispersion, and four-point probe conductivity. The next step is device engineering: stability, adhesion, and encapsulation.
